Short case 20 · General Surgery

Dysphagia

There is nothing to palpate, so the whole case is the history. Four questions carry it: how old, how long, solids first or liquids first, and getting worse or coming and going. Answer those four and you have usually named the lesion before you touch the patient.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1The two definitions, and the one distinction to make first

Dysphagia and odynophagia
SRB: "Dysphagia is difficulty in swallowing. Painful swallowing is odynophagia."​SRB 19 · p.778
Oropharyngeal or oesophageal: ask about coughing, not about the site
SRB draws the line by which phase of swallowing has failed. "Dysphagia may be due to pathology in voluntary/pharyngeal phase of the swallowing wherein patient also develops cough while swallowing. Dysphagia due to problem in oesophageal involuntary phase of swallowing is specified by food getting stuck in the pathway. But site of 'food getting stuck' feeling is not relevant."​SRB 19 · p.778
Why it mattersTwo things follow from that one sentence. Coughing while swallowing localises the problem to the pharyngeal phase, because the protective closure of the larynx is part of that phase and has failed. And where the patient points is worthless, so do not build a differential on it. Candidates lose marks for confidently siting a lesion from the patient's finger.
Odynophagia is a different pointer
Pain on swallowing suggests mucosal inflammation or ulceration, so oesophagitis, candidal oesophagitis or a corrosive injury, rather than a simple obstructing mass. S Das makes the same point from the other direction about cancer: "Pain is conspicuous by its absence."​Das 31 · p.440

2History: every question and what it is for

S Das's eight-point history is the spine of this case. Each step below gives the question and then the discrimination it buys you.

1. How old is the patient? Because age alone shifts the odds more than any other single fact. "Carcinoma of oesophagus is a disease of old age (50 to 70 years)." In infancy the causes are oesophageal atresia, dysphagia lusoria and congenital cardiospasm. In children, a foreign body, paralysis of the soft palate (diphtheria) and acute retropharyngeal abscess. In middle age, benign stricture, achalasia (30 to 40 years) and Paterson-Kelly syndrome.​Das 31 · p.434 In an examOpen with the age bracket and name your top two. It frames everything that follows and examiners read it as clinical maturity.
2. Male or female? One cause is nearly sex-specific. "Paterson-Kelly syndrome (sideropenic dysphagia) occurs almost exclusively in females nearing menopause (over 40 years of age). Achalasia occurs in both sexes though women may dominate. Carcinoma of oesophagus mainly affects men."​Das 31 · p.434 B&L agrees that Plummer-Vinson "is a rare disease, mainly affecting middle-aged women".​B&L 66 · p.1147
3. Solids first, or liquids first? This is the single most discriminating question in the case, and the reason is mechanical. "Difficulty in swallowing first with solids and subsequently with liquids points to mechanical obstruction. This is mainly seen in carcinoma of oesophagus. Difficulty in swallowing first with liquids and subsequently with solids is typical of achalasia (cardiospasm). In the latter condition the weight of the solid helps in overcoming the spasm."​Das 31 · p.434 The mechanism, in one lineA fixed narrowing lets fluid through and stops a bolus, so solids go first. A sphincter that will not relax is overcome by weight and hydrostatic pressure, so a solid bolus can push through where water sits above it. Say the mechanism, not just the pattern. CautionB&L records that achalasia "typically presents with dysphagia (to both solid and liquid)".​B&L 66 · p.1121 So do not reject achalasia because the patient reports trouble with both. The classical liquids-first pattern is a pointer when present, not a requirement.
4. How long, and is it getting worse or coming and going? "A sudden onset may suggest foreign body obstruction or acute oesophagitis. A comparatively short history of difficulty in swallowing (a few months duration) in the elderly suggests carcinoma of oesophagus. A slow onset with a long history obtained in benign stricture, achalasia, pharyngeal pouch etc. Progressively worsening dysphagia is typical of carcinoma and stricture. In case of spastic lesions, (Paterson-Kelly syndrome and Schatzki's rings) there may be periods of remission."​Das 31 · p.434 SRB puts it the same way: in carcinoma "dysphagia is of short duration and progressive".​SRB 19 · p.778 SoShort and relentless in an older patient means cancer. Long and intermittent means a ring, a web or a spasm. A short and intermittent history in a young person suggests a food bolus on a ring. The trapS Das warns of one false reassurance: in cancer, "due to sloughing of a portion of the growth dysphagia may be eased out temporarily".​Das 31 · p.440 A temporary improvement in an elderly patient is not recovery.
5. Is there regurgitation, and how long after eating? The timing separates a pouch and achalasia from reflux. Regurgitation "is often seen in achalasia, but may be seen in sliding hiatus hernia with stooping or straining. Pharyngeal pouch may cause regurgitation. In this case a lump in the neck may be visible which may be emptied with pressure."​Das 31 · p.434 In achalasia, "regurgitation of food even several hours after meal is the main complaint".​Das 31 · p.439 What to ask nextIs the regurgitated material recognisable, undigested food? Then it never reached the stomach, and the hold-up is in the oesophagus or the pouch. Is it sour or bitter? Then it has been in the stomach, and this is reflux. B&L adds the detail that clinches a pouch or a megaoesophagus: "patients may report regurgitating food that they have ingested before", and the retained food ferments, so there is halitosis.​B&L 66 · p.1121
6. Is there pain, and where? "Typical pain along with dysphagia is only complained of in reflux oesophagitis or in corrosive stricture. But majority of patients with dysphagia will complain of some sort of discomfort at the site of obstruction. This type of pain is mainly felt just beneath the sternum."​Das 31 · p.434 Do not over-read the siteS Das says the discomfort is felt "either behind the upper part of the sternum or behind its lower part"​Das 31 · p.434 according to the level, but SRB's warning stands: the sensation of food sticking is not a reliable localiser. Chest pain with dysphagia and no obstruction should raise distal oesophageal spasm, where B&L notes that "patients often undergo extensive investigations before the oesophagus is considered the responsible organ".​B&L 66 · p.1121
7. Is there vomiting, and what is in it? Examine it, and note "the amount, reaction (it is generally not acid in causes other than reflux oesophagitis), odour and presence of blood (carcinoma or oesophageal reflux or very rarely in achalasia)".​Das 31 · p.434 When the oesophagus is dilated, "the patient may complain of vomiting of foul-smelling stagnated intraoesophageal contents of 2 to 3 days old".​Das 31 · p.434 The logicNot acid means it never reached the stomach, so the obstruction is above the cardia. Foul and days old means stasis in a dilated oesophagus, so achalasia or a long-standing stricture. S Das notes regurgitated material in cancer is "usually alkaline mixed with saliva and streaked with blood".​Das 31 · p.441
8. Is there cough, and when in relation to the meal? The interval localises the fistula or the stasis. "Coughing occurring immediately after feeds indicates tracheo-oesophageal fistula. Coughing, which occurs sometime after ingestion of meals may be due to regurgitation of food in case of cardiospasm or pharyngeal pouch."​Das 31 · pp.434, 435 Persistent coughing without this relationship suggests irritation by a mediastinal mass.​Das 31 · p.434 In an older patient, this is a red flagB&L: "choking and cough on drinking water are typical of fistulation and associated haemoptysis is common."​B&L 66 · p.1136 An oesophago-airway fistula in a known cancer means advanced, usually unresectable disease.
9. Has there been weight loss? "This is quite appreciable and is common in achalasia and malignant lesion of the oesophagus."​Das 31 · p.435 So weight loss does not distinguish themThis is worth saying out loud, because candidates reach for weight loss as a cancer marker. B&L is explicit that in achalasia "patients may or may not have experienced weight loss. Frequently, patients will adjust their diet according to symptoms and can maintain their body weight after an initial drop."​B&L 66 · p.1121 Use the rate and the duration, not the fact.
10. Past history: five specific questions Each one names a cause that nothing else will reveal. S Das: "A history of radiation, instrumentation or swallowing of corrosive such as concentrated acid or alkali may be obtained in simple stricture of oesophagus. Past history of vagotomy indicates perioesophagitis to be the cause of dysphagia. Similarly previous history of hiatus hernia repair indicates excessive tightness of the repair to be the cause of dysphagia. Diphtheria may result in dysphagia. Symptoms of other bowel diseases may indicate a rare entity, Crohn's disease of oesophagus."​Das 31 · p.435 Add two more in 2026 practiceDrugs, because SRB lists "KCl, quinine, NSAID" as causes of drug-induced dysphagia;​SRB 19 · p.779 and immunosuppression, since SRB notes oesophageal candidiasis "is becoming common due to immunosuppression in association with HIV infection; steroid therapy; cancer chemotherapy; post-transplant period".​SRB 19 · p.778 Corrosive: which one, and why it mattersSRB: "it is usually alkali stricture. Squamous mucosa is resistant to acid effect to certain extent."​SRB 19 · p.778 So ask specifically whether the substance swallowed was an acid or an alkali. B&L lists lye corrosive stricture among the aetiological factors for squamous cell cancer, so this history has a long tail as well.​B&L 66 · p.1136

3Examination: what there is to find, and why you still do it

Before you touch the patient The examiner is marking this before you have found anything. Bailey & Love gives it as a sequence: "ensure you have followed appropriate hand hygiene guidance. Introduce yourself and check the patient's name and date of birth. Request presence of a chaperone as appropriate. Explain what you are going to do, obtain verbal consent and ensure that the patient is comfortable."​B&L 35 · p.472 And the standard it is held to: "patients should be treated with respect and dignity, receive a clear explanation of the examination undertaken and be kept as comfortable as possible. A chaperone should be present, especially for intimate examinations."​B&L 21 · p.285

Do it, and be heard doing itWash your hands. Introduce yourself. Say what you want to examine and why, and ask permission. Ask for a chaperone where the examination is intimate. Expose what you need and cover the rest. Warm your hands. Tell the patient what each step will feel like and that they can ask you to stop, examine the tender part last, and watch their face rather than only your hands. Cover them and thank them before you turn to the examiner.
General survey, four findings
"Emaciation is usual in a case of dysphagia but is much more prominent in case of achalasia and malignant diseases. Anaemia is very much evident in Paterson-Kelly syndrome and carcinoma of oesophagus and in reflux oesophagitis. Radial pulses will be inequal on two sides in case of aneurysm of the aorta. Concave and spoon-shaped nail is peculiar of Paterson-Kelly syndrome. The tongue is also smooth, pale and devoid of papillae in Paterson-Kelly syndrome."​Das 31 · p.435
Why unequal radial pulsesBecause an aneurysm of the aortic arch can both compress the oesophagus and alter flow into one subclavian. It is the one cause of dysphagia you diagnose at the wrist.
Mouth and pharynx
"Tonsils and fauces should be examined for any lesion. Test the mobility of the soft palate to determine if it is paralysed or not. The posterior wall of the pharynx is examined to exclude retropharyngeal abscess."​Das 31 · p.435 Three causes, three findings, none of which needs any instrument.
The neck, and the one swelling that appears while you watch
"A soft swelling which appear during meals just above the left clavicle is the third stage of pharyngeal pouch. Pressure over such swelling will cause regurgitation of food into the mouth."​Das 31 · p.435 B&L explains why the left: "most diverticula point towards the left side", which is also why the operation is through a left cervical incision.​B&L 66 · p.1127 SRB adds the bedside sign: "when the patient drinks the pouch can be seen to be enlarging with gurgling noise in the neck" is S Das's version of it.​Das 31 · p.439
Tracheal tuggingS Das's technique, for an arch aneurysm: "the clinician stands behind the patient and holds the cricoid cartilage with a little upward traction. The downward tug can be felt with each throb of the aorta."​Das 31 · p.435
And the one you must not omit"If no relevant sign can be elicited on examination of the neck one must palpate the left supraclavicular fossa to exclude presence of enlarged lymph nodes which may be the only sign in case of carcinoma of the oesophagus."​Das 31 · p.435 B&L supplies the anatomy behind it: the thoracic duct drains into the junction of the left jugular and left subclavian veins, which "explains the finding of Virchow's node (Troisier's sign), when a metastatic node is found in the left supraclavicular fossa, both from intra-abdominal malignancies as well as from oesophageal cancer".​B&L 66 · p.1108
Chest
"In majority of cases there will be hardly any abnormality." But look for pleural effusion in a late cancer, and for "aspiration pneumonitis, which may cause lung abscess, bronchiectasis, haemoptysis" in achalasia.​Das 31 · p.435 SRB puts recurrent pneumonia in achalasia at 60% and names lung abscess as a complication.​SRB 19 · p.789
Abdomen, and the spine
Abdomen: look for a mass from a cancer infiltrating the upper stomach, and an enlarged liver from metastases in carcinoma of the cardia.​Das 31 · p.435 Spine: "if Pott's disease is suspected to cause dysphagia due to its cold abscess pressing on the pharynx or oesophagus one should examine the cervical region of the spine."​Das 31 · p.435 Rare, and free to look for.
The one-line summary of the examination There is nothing to feel in the chest, so the examination is a search for the complication and for the metastasis, not for the lesion. Nails and tongue for Paterson-Kelly, left supraclavicular fossa for Virchow's node, chest for aspiration, abdomen for liver and a mass. Say that aloud at the start of your examination and the examiner knows you understand why you are doing it.

4Causes, in the frame examiners expect

S Das classifies by site, then within the oesophagus by lumen, wall, outside the wall. SRB uses the same three columns and adds a fourth for neurological causes. Learn one and you can write either.

SiteIn the lumenIn the wallOutside the wall
MouthTonsillitis, quinsy, stomatitis, carcinoma of the tongue, paralysis of the soft palate (diphtheria in children, bulbar palsy in adults)
PharynxImpacted foreign body: coin, tooth, denture Acute pharyngitis; malignant growth; hysterical spasm; Paterson-Kelly syndrome Retropharyngeal abscess; enlarged cervical node; malignant thyroid
OesophagusImpacted foreign body Atresia; benign stricture (reflux, corrosive, tuberculosis, scleroderma, radiotherapy); spasm (Paterson-Kelly, achalasia, webs and rings, diffuse oesophageal spasm); diverticulum; neoplasm, mainly malignant; nervous disorders (bulbar palsy, post-vagotomy); Crohn's disease Malignant or large thyroid, retrosternal goitre; pharyngeal diverticulum; aortic aneurysm; mediastinal growth; dysphagia lusoria; perioesophagitis after vagotomy; paraoesophageal (type II) hiatus hernia; too tight an oesophageal hiatus repair

S Das ch.31 pp.437. SRB ch.19 p.779 gives the same table with a separate column of cranial or neurological causes: bulbar palsy, infarction or hemiplegia, vertebrobasilar insufficiency; and adds oesophageal candidiasis, Boerhaave's syndrome, motor neuron disease, Parkinson's disease, drug-induced dysphagia and mediastinal fibrosis (SRB ch.19 pp.778, 779).

If you are asked for the five commonest, not the full list SRB's own "common causes" are shorter and better for a viva: gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, carcinoma oesophagus, foreign body, carcinoma of the pharynx or posterior third of the tongue, corrosive stricture, oesophageal candidiasis, and Plummer-Vinson syndrome.​SRB 19 · p.778 Everything else SRB files under rare.

5Investigations

Where to start, in one sentence
Endoscopy, in almost every adult. It sees the mucosa, it takes the biopsy, and it is the only test that can both diagnose and treat at the same sitting. The books do not fully agree on this and the first amber box below sets out why, but the ruling is not in doubt for an adult with progressive dysphagia.
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
"Endoscopy is an essential tool with both diagnostic and therapeutic roles. A standard diagnostic upper endoscopy includes the examination of the pharynx, hypopharynx, laryngeal inlet, oesophagus, stomach and part of the duodenum."​B&L 66 · p.1108
Two safety points worth a mark each"Extra care should be taken when performing endoscopy for patients with achalasia or obstruction as the oesophagus can be fluid-filled and regurgitation may lead to aspiration."​B&L 66 · p.1108 And where perforation is suspected or the procedure will be long, "carbon dioxide should be used for insufflation since it is absorbed more quickly than air".​B&L 66 · p.1109
And one negative that is not reassuringIn achalasia, "a normal endoscopy however does not exclude achalasia, as 30 to 40% of endoscopies are reported as normal before a final diagnosis of achalasia is made".​B&L 66 · p.1122 Its real value there is to exclude pseudo-achalasia, meaning "cancer of the gastric cardia mimicking achalasia".​B&L 66 · p.1122
Chromoendoscopy and image enhancement, for early disease
Lugol's iodine 0.5 to 1% to look for "any suspicious unstained areas and pink colour sign in squamous neoplasia"; acetic acid 1 to 3% for "loss of aceto-whitening" in Barrett's mucosa and neoplasia.​B&L 66 · p.1109 The principle is simple and worth stating: normal squamous mucosa takes up iodine, dysplastic and early cancerous mucosa does not.​B&L 66 · p.1136
Contrast swallow
Still the test that shows you shape, level and motion in one picture. "A barium contrast swallow can demonstrate narrowing, anatomical distortion or abnormal oesophageal motility."​B&L 66 · p.1108 It is the right first test where you suspect a pharyngeal pouch (and S Das insists on a thin emulsion, since "thick mixture refuses to be washed out from the pouch following examination")​Das 31 · p.439 or a high stricture, where passing a scope blind risks perforation.
And the one thing it must not be used for"It is however inaccurate in the diagnosis of GORD and should not be used for this purpose."​B&L 66 · p.1108
The barium appearances you must be able to describe
Carcinoma: "the dilatation of the oesophagus above the tumour is less marked. Moreover, the constricted part is extremely irregular (the filling defect which is often called 'rat-tail' deformity) and a 'shouldering' may be seen at the proximal end of the filling defect. A soft tissue shadow of the tumour can be obtained."​Das 31 · p.436
Benign stricture: "a long tortuous stricture with some dilatation of the proximal oesophagus and without any shouldering at the proximal end of the stricture."​Das 31 · p.439 So shouldering is the discriminator, and absence of it with a long smooth narrowing says benign.
Achalasia: "the distal 'bird-beak' taper of the oesophagogastric junction at the distal end of the dilated oesophagus", with retained contents and, in late disease, massive dilatation and tortuosity.​Das 31 · p.436 SRB adds the two signs candidates forget: absence of the fundic gas bubble​SRB 19 · p.789 (because no air passes the sphincter, which B&L explains directly)​B&L 66 · p.1121 and the late sigmoid oesophagus.​SRB 19 · p.789
Diffuse oesophageal spasm: a corkscrew oesophagus.​B&L 66 · p.1125
Careful with "rat-tail"S Das uses rat-tail for the irregular narrowing of carcinoma;​Das 31 · p.436 B&L uses "rat's tail" as a synonym for bird's beak in achalasia.​B&L 66 · p.1122 Say bird's beak for achalasia and irregular filling defect with shouldering for cancer, and you cannot be misunderstood.
Manometry
For motility, not for obstruction. It shows in achalasia "failure of LES to relax reflexly with swallowing and lack of progressive peristalsis throughout the length of the oesophagus", and in diffuse oesophageal spasm "multiphasic, repetitive and high-amplitude contractions that occur after swallowing".​Das 31 · p.437 B&L: "definitive diagnosis relies on HRM",​B&L 66 · p.1122 and in its own summary box, "HRM is the gold standard for the diagnosis of oesophageal motility disorder".​B&L 66 · p.1125 See the second amber box for what HRM is and why the old thresholds have gone.
pH studies
For reflux, where barium is unreliable. S Das: "pH recording in the oesophagus 5 cm above the distal oesophageal high-pressure zone shows decline in pH to less than 4, which is a clear evidence of gastro-oesophageal reflux."​Das 31 · p.437 SRB: "24 hours pH monitoring is ideal and most accurate for GERD."​SRB 19 · p.779
CT, and endoscopic ultrasound
Not for making the diagnosis, for staging it. "Computed tomography scanning is important in the staging of a malignant neoplasm, delineating the anatomical relationship with other mediastinal structures."​B&L 66 · p.1108 EUS gives "highly detailed images of the layers of the oesophageal wall", so it is the test for T stage and for sampling adjacent nodes.​B&L 66 · p.1110 S Das's blunt verdict on CT for diagnosis still holds: "the value of these investigations is not much in finding out the cause of dysphagia".​Das 31 · p.437
Blood, and the one you will be asked for
Haemoglobin and iron studies, because iron deficiency anaemia is both a cause (Plummer-Vinson) and a consequence (chronic blood loss from a tumour, which B&L notes is less common for squamous cell cancer than adenocarcinoma).​B&L 66 · p.1136
Barium swallow first, or endoscopy first? A live disagreement, and the most consequential one in this case. S Das 31 p.436 calls barium "by far the most important investigation in dysphagia"; B&L 66 p.1108 relegates contrast to one paragraph and makes endoscopy the essential tool
S Das
Unambiguous: "Radiography with barium meal. This is by far the most important investigation in dysphagia. More or less all the conditions which may give rise to dysphagia will be diagnosed by this investigation."​Das 31 · p.436 Three pages of the chapter are given to the appearances, and oesophagoscopy is listed second. S Das also treats rigid oesophagoscopy as a working tool, both diagnostic and therapeutic: in benign stricture "this investigation not only helps in the diagnosis but also can be used to dilate the stricture with an oesophageal bougie".​Das 31 · p.436
SRB
Sits in the middle. It still leads with barium for achalasia, "barium swallow is diagnostic",​SRB 19 · p.789 but it requires oesophagoscopy "to confirm the diagnosis and to rule out carcinoma oesophagus" with "biopsy of mucosa at LES".​SRB 19 · p.790
Bailey & Love 28e
The phrase "barium swallow" appears once in the whole 42-page chapter, and then only as a parameter used to plan the length of a POEM myotomy.​B&L 66 · p.1124 Contrast studies get a single paragraph under Radiography, and carry an explicit prohibition for GORD.​B&L 66 · p.1108 Endoscopy gets three pages and the opening line "endoscopy is an essential tool with both diagnostic and therapeutic roles".​B&L 66 · p.1108 And on S Das's rigid instrument B&L is categorical: "rigid oesophagoscopy is rarely used nowadays except for unusual circumstances, such as retrieving large or sharp foreign objects."​B&L 66 · p.1109
Why the two books diverged
Not a disagreement about what barium shows. It is that barium cannot biopsy, and the one diagnosis you cannot afford to delay in an adult with progressive dysphagia is cancer. A flexible endoscope reaches the same diagnosis and leaves with histology, so the extra step has become hard to justify where endoscopy is available. S Das is a clinical-method text written around what a bedside clinician can obtain and interpret, and in that frame barium earns its place.
How to answer: lead with endoscopy and give barium a named indication, which is the position all three books can be read as supporting. "In an adult with progressive dysphagia I would do an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy first, because it visualises the mucosa and gives me a biopsy at the same sitting, and carcinoma is the diagnosis I must exclude. I would ask for a contrast swallow first in three situations: a suspected pharyngeal pouch, where blind intubation risks perforating the pouch and where a thin barium emulsion is needed; a suspected high or tight stricture, to show me the level and length before anything is passed; and a suspected motility disorder, where the contrast study shows me the dynamics that endoscopy cannot." If the examiner is from the older school and presses barium first, do not fight: say that barium remains the test that shows level, length and motility in one image, and that you would still need endoscopy for tissue. Never say rigid oesophagoscopy unless you are retrieving a foreign body.
Manometry: is the diagnostic standard an LOS pressure over 35 mmHg, or the Chicago classification on high-resolution manometry? A framework that has moved, not a disagreement about physiology. SRB 19 p.790 teaches conventional manometry with pressure thresholds; B&L 66 pp.1110, 1121 has replaced it with HRM and Chicago 4.0
SRB
Conventional manometry, with a number to quote: "oesophageal manometry shows unrelaxed lower oesophageal sphincter with high resting pressure, very useful and gold standard. It shows failure of LES to relax completely during swallowing and complete absence of peristalsis. LES pressure is >35 mmHg."​SRB 19 · p.790 S Das describes the same test in the same terms, without a threshold.​Das 31 · p.437
Bailey & Love 28e
Describes conventional water-perfused manometry as history: "with the introduction of the colour contour plot by Ray Clouse in 1995, conventional manometry is gradually being replaced by high-resolution manometry (HRM) with solid-state pressure catheters. A typical HRM catheter has 36 circumferential sensors along its length, each spaced 1 cm apart."​B&L 66 · p.1110 The measurement that matters is no longer a resting pressure but the integrated relaxation pressure (IRP), "the relaxation pressure across the OGJ in response to a swallow".​B&L 66 · p.1121 An abnormal IRP puts the patient in disorders of OGJ outflow, which contains the three types of achalasia and OGJ outflow obstruction; a normal one sends you to disorders of peristalsis: absent contractility, distal oesophageal spasm, hypercontractile oesophagus and ineffective oesophageal motility.​B&L 66 · p.1121
Why it is not merely cosmetic
The three types of achalasia change management, which no pressure threshold did. B&L: "in type III achalasia, there is a spastic component at the distal oesophagus that responds less well to pneumatic dilatation and Heller's myotomy", and POEM is preferred there because "it can extend the length of the myotomy proximally".​B&L 66 · p.1124 Its summary box states it plainly: "type III achalasia may be better treated with long myotomy by POEM."​B&L 66 · p.1125 B&L also notes that "all motility disorders have to be associated with symptoms or other supporting tests to make them clinically relevant", so a manometric label alone does not justify treatment.​B&L 66 · p.1121
How to answer: both are safe, because the clinical finding has not changed. Say the finding first, then the modern framework. "Manometry shows failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax on swallowing with absent peristalsis in the oesophageal body. Classically this was a raised resting sphincter pressure, over 35 mmHg on conventional manometry. Current practice uses high-resolution manometry, which measures the integrated relaxation pressure and classifies motility disorders under the Chicago classification; a raised IRP defines a disorder of oesophagogastric junction outflow, of which there are three types of achalasia." Add the consequence if you have the chance, because it is the only part an examiner cannot get from an older book: type III achalasia has a spastic distal segment and is better treated by a long myotomy, usually POEM. For a written answer in India, give SRB's description and threshold, then one sentence on HRM and the Chicago classification.

6The conditions you must be able to separate

Achalasia cardia
What it is. "The term achalasia originated from the Greek word 'khalasis', meaning 'failure to relax'."​B&L 66 · p.1121 S Das: "this represents failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax with deglutition. The number of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus seems to be diminished."​Das 31 · p.439
The mechanism, in B&L's words, which is worth learning whole. "The mismatch in excitatory and inhibitory activity results in the failure of LOS relaxation and absent peristalsis. With time, the oesophagus dilates and contractions disappear, so that the oesophagus empties mainly by the hydrostatic pressure of its contents. This is nearly always incomplete, leaving residual food and fluid."​B&L 66 · p.1121 That sentence explains the regurgitation, the halitosis, the aspiration and the missing fundic gas bubble at once.
Aetiology. "The aetiology remains uncertain but is postulated to be due to loss of the inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, possibly related to a virus-induced autoimmune effect."​B&L 66 · p.1121 SRB adds the chemistry: "reduced nitric oxide and VIP (mediators of LES relaxation)".​SRB 19 · p.789
Two named associations. Chagas' disease, where "chronic infection with the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi" destroys the myenteric plexus in South America; and Allgrove syndrome, "a rare genetic syndrome associated with familial adrenal insufficiency, alacrimia and achalasia".​B&L 66 · p.1121
The triad SRB wants. Dysphagia, regurgitation, weight loss.​SRB 19 · p.789
Vigorous achalasia, a term SRB uses and B&L does not: "achalasia with diffuse oesophageal spasm is called as 'vigorous achalasia' (achalasia with high amplitude contractions)".​SRB 19 · p.789
The bedside manoeuvres patients inventSRB lists them, and they make a memorable answer: "walking while eating, chin thrusting, neck and shoulder extension, Valsalva manoeuvre facilitates emptying of food from the oesophagus."​SRB 19 · p.789 All of them raise intraoesophageal hydrostatic pressure, which is the only emptying mechanism left.
Pseudoachalasia, which you must exclude: "features like achalasia cardia with dysphagia and weight loss, seen in an elderly due to carcinoma. Amyl nitrate inhalation causes sphincter relaxation in achalasia cardia but not in pseudoachalasia."​SRB 19 · p.791 B&L makes the same point, that endoscopy is "an important investigation to exclude 'pseudo-achalasia', often referring to cancer of the gastric cardia mimicking achalasia".​B&L 66 · p.1122
Achalasia: treatment, and what the goal is
Say the goal first, because it reframes everything: "the treatment goal of achalasia is for symptom palliation since there is no therapy to reverse the neuronal degeneration. Therapies target the LOS, aiming to reduce its contractility by pharmacological means or by destroying the muscle fibres using endoscopic or surgical methods."​B&L 66 · p.1122
Drugs: calcium channel blockers, nitrates, phosphodiesterase inhibitors. "Most have limited efficacy... medical therapy should be reserved for selected patients who are poor candidates for endoscopic or surgical treatments."​B&L 66 · p.1122
Botulinum toxin: "the reported symptom relief decreased from 70% in 3 months to around 40% in a year", so it is repeated, and "repeated injection may result in scarring, making subsequent treatments more difficult". B&L restricts it: "it should not be offered as first-line treatment in patients who are suitable for myotomy or pneumatic dilatation and its indication is usually restricted to elderly patients with comorbidities."​B&L 66 · p.1123
Pneumatic dilatation: balloons of 30 to 40 mm over a guidewire, graded up. B&L names the responders: "patients older than 45 years, female, those with an undilated oesophagus, those who have responded to first dilatation and those with type II achalasia."​B&L 66 · p.1123
Heller's myotomy: "anterior myotomy is performed for at least 6 cm proximally at the oesophageal side and 2–3 cm distally into the gastric cardia... currently, the standard procedure is a laparoscopic approach."​B&L 66 · pp.1123, 1124 SRB's figures are 8 to 10 cm of circular muscle, "2 cm proximal to the thickened muscle to 1 cm distal to OG junction", with the warning "care should be taken not to open the mucosa", and the historical note that "original Heller's is both anterior and posterior myotomies" while anterior alone is done now.​SRB 19 · p.790
Why you must add a fundoplication, and why not a Nissen "The major complication is GORD, which can occur in up to 40% of patients. The addition of a partial fundoplication (anterior Dor or posterior Toupet) has been shown to be effective in reducing the incidence of GORD. A complete 360° fundoplication (Nissen) is considered contraindicated because the increase in outflow resistance against an aperistaltic oesophageal body will probably result in postoperative dysphagia."​B&L 66 · p.1124 That last clause is the whole answer: the oesophagus above has no peristalsis to push against a full wrap.
POEM: submucosal tunnel, then myotomy of the circular muscle from inside, closed with endoclips; "randomised controlled trials have demonstrated similar efficacy of POEM to pneumatic dilatation and Heller's myotomy in relieving dysphagia". Its cost is reflux: without an antireflux procedure, "the incidence of oesophagitis at 3 months after POEM can be as high as 57%, which may subject patients to lifelong acid suppression therapy or subsequent antireflux operation."​B&L 66 · p.1124
Oesophagectomy: "reserved only for the treatment of patients with 'end-stage' achalasia with a sigmoidal or megaoesophagus that is not responding to other methods."​B&L 66 · p.1124 SRB agrees, naming transhiatal total oesophagectomy with gastric pull-up for megaoesophagus or metaplasia.​SRB 19 · p.790
Carcinoma of the oesophagus
Who. "It should be suspected when a man above 40 years complains of heaviness or oppression behind the sternum at the time of meals."​Das 31 · p.440 B&L: "it most commonly presents in the sixth and seventh decades of life", and oesophageal cancer is "the eighth most common cancer worldwide and the sixth most common cause of cancer death".​B&L 66 · p.1135
Which cell type, and where. "Squamous cell cancers tend to be found in the middle and upper part of the oesophagus, while adenocarcinoma predominantly affects the lower oesophagus and OGJ."​B&L 66 · p.1136 And the geography, which matters for an Indian answer: "squamous cell cancer still predominates in the East, while Barrett's adenocarcinoma is more common in the West",​B&L 66 · p.1146 with the shift in the West dated: "among white populations, especially in developed Western countries, there has been an epidemiological shift since the 1990s from squamous cell carcinoma to adenocarcinoma such that the incidence of adenocarcinoma has surpassed that of squamous cell cancer."​B&L 66 · p.1135
Risk factors, split by cell type, which is how B&L tabulates them and how you should recite them.​B&L 66 · p.1136 For squamous: smoking, alcohol, hot beverages, N-nitroso-containing food such as pickled vegetables, chewing betel nut, yerba mate, dietary deficiency of fresh green vegetables, fruit and vitamins, low socioeconomic class, fungal toxin or virus, radiation to the mediastinum, lye corrosive stricture, previous upper aerodigestive malignancy, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, achalasia. For adenocarcinoma: Barrett's oesophagus (the strongest), gastro-oesophageal reflux, obesity, smoking and alcohol to a lesser degree.
Two mechanisms worth knowingThe ALDH2 story explains the East Asian flushing association: "alcohol is metabolised to acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase and the acetaldehyde is in turn metabolised by ALDH2 to acetate. Individuals with variants of the ALDH2 gene may have a suboptimal level of the enzyme, leading to the accumulation of the carcinogen acetaldehyde."​B&L 66 · p.1135 And the second primary risk: "using oesophageal cancer as the index tumour, multiple primary cancers are found in about 10% of patients, of which 70% are in the aerodigestive tract."​B&L 66 · p.1136
Why it presents late, and spreads early. "The oesophageal wall has a rich network of submucosal lymphatics, and therefore longitudinal submucosal spread of cancer is common."​B&L 66 · p.1136 B&L draws the surgical conclusion: "a longer resection margin reduces the chance of local recurrence",​B&L 66 · p.1108 and the wall "lacks a serosa",​B&L 66 · p.1107 so there is no barrier to early local invasion. Note also that nodal spread "can be unpredictable and skip lesions can occur",​B&L 66 · p.1108 which is the rationale for three-field lymphadenectomy.
Late complications to name. Hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement; broncho-oesophageal fistula; and "erosion of aorta, though very rare, is a fatal complication".​Das 31 · p.441 B&L describes how aorto-oesophageal fistula kills: "usually presents with a smaller sentinel bleed followed by massive bleeding that is invariably fatal."​B&L 66 · p.1136
Palliation, which is what most Indian patients will need: "placement of a self-expanding metallic stent is simple and effective and allows immediate relief of dysphagia. The risks are stent migration, tumour ingrowth, airway compression and tracheal erosion if placed in the mid- and upper oesophagus."​B&L 66 · p.1146
Plummer-Vinson or Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome
The name. B&L gives both and explains the split: "Plummer-Vinson (in the USA) or Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome (UK) refers to the findings of a cervical oesophageal web, iron deficiency anaemia and dysphagia. It is also known as sideropenic dysphagia."​B&L 66 · pp.1146, 1147 S Das gives the dates: "first described by Paterson and Kelly in 1919 and subsequently more elaborately described by Plummer and Vinson in 1921."​Das 31 · p.438
The clinical picture. "The patient is nearly always a middle-aged woman who presents with difficulty in swallowing. Glossitis, anaemia and dysphagia form the important triad of this disease. The tongue becomes devoid of papillae, smooth and pale. The lips and corners of the mouth are often cracked. Hypochromic anaemia is almost always present. The nails become brittle and spoon shaped (koilonychia)."​Das 31 · p.438 SRB adds cheilitis and notes splenomegaly may be present.​SRB 19 · p.791
Why it is premalignant, and where. S Das: "this lesion is considered to be pre-cancerous."​Das 31 · p.438 B&L is more precise about the site: "there is a predisposition to postcricoid, cervical oesophageal cancer."​B&L 66 · p.1147
Treatment. "Treatment is with iron therapy, diet modification and, if necessary, endoscopic dilatation of the cervical web."​B&L 66 · p.1147 SRB gives the dose: ferrous sulphate 300 mg three times a day with vitamins,​SRB 19 · p.791 and insists on oesophagoscopy and biopsy to rule out malignancy.​SRB 19 · p.791
Web or ring?B&L's distinction is histological and is a favourite viva question: "a web is distinguished from a Schatzki's ring in that both the proximal and distal surfaces of the web are lined by squamous mucosa; in a Schatzki's ring, the proximal side is lined with squamous mucosa and the distal side by columnar mucosa, coinciding with its location at the squamocolumnar junction."​B&L 66 · p.1147 Both narrow the lumen; one sits at the top of the oesophagus and one at the bottom.
Schatzki's ring, and the 13 mm rule
A mucosal band at the squamocolumnar junction, "not an uncommon cause of food impaction in adults". The number to quote: "radiological studies using barium contrast by Schatzki demonstrated that, in individuals with a ring size of less than 13 mm, the symptom of dysphagia may occur."​B&L 66 · p.1147 S Das gives the same threshold.​Das 31 · p.440 Aetiology "is uncertain but is believed to be related to GORD; hiatus hernia is more common", and treatment is endoscopic dilatation if symptomatic.​B&L 66 · p.1147
Pharyngeal pouch, Zenker's diverticulum
Where and why. "Zenker's diverticulum is a false pulsion diverticulum as it protrudes posteriorly above the cricopharyngeal sphincter through the natural weak point (the dehiscence of Killian) between the oblique and horizontal fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. The pathophysiology is believed to involve loss of coordination between pharyngeal contraction and opening of the upper sphincter."​B&L 66 · p.1126 S Das names the two parts of the muscle: the oblique thyropharyngeal and the transverse cricopharyngeal.​Das 31 · p.438
False, and pulsion. Both books insist on this: it is a herniation of mucosa and submucosa through a weakened area, so the muscle is not in the wall of the pouch.​Das 31 · p.438​B&L 66 · p.1126
How it presents, in order. "When the diverticulum is small, symptoms largely reflect desynchronisation of swallowing with predominantly pharyngeal dysphagia. As the pouch enlarges, it tends to fill with food on eating, and the fundus descends into the mediastinum. Regurgitation of trapped food can occur and lead to aspiration. Another symptom is halitosis."​B&L 66 · p.1127 S Das adds the one that wakes the patient: "sometimes the patients may wake up from sleep with a feeling of suffocation followed by a severe cough."​Das 31 · p.439
Treatment. "Conventional surgical treatment involves an open left cervical incision (most diverticula point towards the left side) with diverticulectomy and cricopharyngeus myotomy." The alternative is diverticular suspension, inverting the pouch apex upwards, whose advantage is that "the absence of a suture line lessens the chance of a postoperative leak". Newer: a transoral linear stapler dividing the septum between pouch and lumen, where "the myotomy is in effect performed by the stapler transection".​B&L 66 · p.1127
The one step that is never optionalCricopharyngeus myotomy. B&L says it twice, calling it "an integral part of the surgery".​B&L 66 · p.1127 The reason is the pathophysiology: excise the pouch and leave the failing sphincter, and you have left the cause behind.
The other two diverticula, in one line each
Midoesophageal (Rokitansky): a traction diverticulum, hence a true one with all layers, pulled out by "fibrosis or lymphadenopathy in the mediastinum" in granulomatous disease, and "rarely it may cause fistulation into the airway in uncontrolled pulmonary tuberculosis". Asymptomatic ones need no treatment.​B&L 66 · p.1127 S Das: usually from tuberculous lymph nodes near the tracheal bifurcation.​Das 31 · p.439
Epiphrenic: a pulsion diverticulum "typically situated at the distal 10 cm of the oesophagus" and "commonly associated with oesophageal motility disorders, e.g. achalasia". Large ones are "excised combined with a myotomy from the neck of the diverticulum to the cardia to relieve the functional obstruction".​B&L 66 · p.1127 Same principle as the pouch: treat the motility disorder or the diverticulum comes back.
Dysphagia lusoria
The embryology. SRB: "it is due to disappearance of proximal right 4th aortic arch instead of distal portion. All patients having this anomaly (dysphagia lusoria) have got an aberrant right subclavian artery in a transposed position arising from descending aorta that courses posterior to oesophagus."​SRB 19 · p.779 S Das describes the same mechanism and notes the artery may rarely run in front of the oesophagus or in front of the trachea.​Das 31 · p.441
The name. SRB: "lusoria means in Latin 'sport of nature'."​SRB 19 · p.779
Investigations and treatment. "CT chest, MRI, chest X-ray, barium swallow (T4 level diagonal impression) and endoscopy (shows pulsating extraluminal compressive mass)"; "treatment is reconstruction or ligation of aberrant right subclavian artery by sternotomy or by neck approach."​SRB 19 · p.779
And a conflict about ageSee the amber box below: S Das files it under infancy, SRB says it usually presents after 40, and B&L 28e does not mention it at all.
Oesophageal atresia with distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula
"This is the commonest form of oesophageal atresia occurring in about 90% of patients. The proximal oesophagus ends as a blind tube and the distal oesophagus is joined to the lower part of the trachea." Presentation: "the infant has an abundance of saliva which may bubble out from the mouth. 'Spitting up' or frank vomiting during feeding is a characteristic sign. Aspiration, choking, cyanosis and respiratory distress are often noticed." Diagnosis: "attempts to push a nasogastric tube will be stopped at the upper mediastinum", and a plain film with a radio-opaque tube tip in situ makes the diagnosis, with intestinal gas confirming the distal fistula. The danger: "a great possibility of aspiration of gastric juice, which is highly injurious to the lungs."​Das 31 · pp.437, 438 Antenatally, look for hydramnios.​Das 31 · p.437
Scleroderma, and the reason it hits the lower oesophagus
"Oesophageal motor disturbances occur in scleroderma or systemic sclerosis. This is due to fibrous replacement of oesophageal smooth muscle and then the distal oesophagus loses its tone and normal response to swallowing and gastro-oesophageal reflux occurs."​Das 31 · p.439 B&L supplies the anatomy that explains the distribution: the upper third is striated muscle, the lower third smooth, and "connective tissue disease, such as scleroderma, mainly affects smooth muscle, hence the lower oesophagus".​B&L 66 · p.1107
Is achalasia premalignant, and if so by how much? A live disagreement in strength of claim. SRB 19 p.789 gives a relative risk and a percentage; B&L 66 p.1121 says only that it "may predispose"; S Das 31 p.439 does not raise it
SRB
States it as established, with numbers: "achalasia cardia is a precancerous condition, seven times chances of getting squamous cell carcinoma (8%, after 15 years)."​SRB 19 · p.789 SRB also acts on it, listing resection for metaplasia among the indications for oesophagectomy.​SRB 19 · p.790
Bailey & Love 28e
Gives the mechanism and then hedges the conclusion: "persistent retention oesophagitis due to fermentation of food residues may predispose to the increased incidence of carcinoma of the oesophagus."​B&L 66 · p.1121 No relative risk, no percentage, no surveillance recommendation anywhere in the chapter. B&L does, however, list achalasia in its table of aetiological factors for squamous cell cancer,​B&L 66 · p.1136 so it accepts the association while declining to quantify it.
S Das
Describes achalasia over a page and lists its complications as "pneumonia, bronchiectasis and lung abscess". Malignancy is not among them.​Das 31 · p.439
What is actually in dispute
Nobody disputes the association or the mechanism: stasis, fermentation, chronic retention oesophagitis, chronic inflammation, squamous dysplasia. What is disputed is whether the absolute risk is high enough to act on. An 8% risk at 15 years would justify endoscopic surveillance; a vague elevation over a low baseline in an uncommon disease would not, and B&L recommends none.
How to answer: affirm the association, give SRB's figures as figures, and attribute them. "Yes. Achalasia is a recognised premalignant condition for squamous cell carcinoma. The mechanism is stasis of fermenting food causing persistent retention oesophagitis. SRB quotes a sevenfold increase, around 8% at fifteen years. Bailey and Love lists achalasia among the aetiological factors for squamous cell cancer but puts it no more strongly than that it may predispose, and recommends no surveillance programme." Then give the practical consequence, which is what the examiner is really after: in any patient with achalasia, particularly an older one, endoscopy and biopsy are done to exclude malignancy before treatment, both because of this risk and because of pseudoachalasia. Quote the 8% as SRB's number, not as a fact everyone agrees on.
Pneumatic dilatation: what is the risk of perforation? A live numerical disagreement. SRB 19 p.790 gives 5%; B&L 66 p.1123 gives an average of 1.9% and under 0.5% with a 30 mm balloon
SRB
For Plummer's pneumatic dilatation with 30 to 40 mm balloons: "risk of perforation (5%), need for repeated dilatations are the problems." And for the Negus hydrostatic method, "it is not very well accepted method as chances of perforation is high. Success rate is 65%."​SRB 19 · p.790
Bailey & Love 28e
Gives a pooled figure with its spread and then makes it dose-dependent on balloon size: "perforation is uncommon; the reported incidence averaged about 1.9% (0 to 16%). With a 30-mm balloon, the chance of perforation should be less than 0.5%. The risk of perforation increases with bigger balloons, which should be used cautiously for progressive dilatation over weeks." It adds the safety requirement: "it is important to have an experienced endoscopist performing the procedure and surgical back-up in case of perforation."​B&L 66 · p.1123 B&L also notes that iatrogenic perforation from endoscopic dilatation of strictures or achalasia is the most common cause of oesophageal perforation overall.​B&L 66 · p.1127
Why the numbers differ
They are not measuring the same thing. SRB quotes one figure for the procedure; B&L quotes a mean across series whose own range runs from 0 to 16%, and then separates out the balloon size, which is the variable that actually drives the risk. SRB's 5% sits comfortably inside B&L's range. The Negus hydrostatic dilator that SRB describes, and which it says has a high perforation rate, does not appear in B&L 28e at all, so part of SRB's higher number may belong to an older and more dangerous technique.
How to answer: give the figure with its condition attached, which is both safer and more impressive than either number alone. "Perforation is the serious complication. Reported rates average around 2% but range widely between series. The risk depends on balloon diameter: under 0.5% with a 30 mm balloon, and rising with larger ones, which is why dilatation is graded from 30 to 35 to 40 mm over weeks rather than done in one sitting. SRB quotes 5%. It should be done by an experienced endoscopist with surgical back-up." If asked for a single number in a written paper, write SRB's 5% and add in brackets that larger series average closer to 2% and that it is balloon-size dependent.
Plummer-Vinson: is the iron deficiency the cause, or just an association? A live disagreement about mechanism. S Das 31 p.438 makes the anaemia part of the defining triad; B&L 66 p.1147 calls the association itself controversial
S Das and SRB
Both treat the iron deficiency as central. S Das: "glossitis, anaemia and dysphagia form the important triad of this disease... hypochromic anaemia is almost always present", and the dysphagia itself is attributed to "spasm of the circular muscle fibres at the extreme upper portion of the oesophagus".​Das 31 · p.438 SRB: "common in patients with long-standing iron deficiency anaemia", and its only medical treatment is iron.​SRB 19 · p.791
Bailey & Love 28e
Keeps iron deficiency in the definition, "the findings of a cervical oesophageal web, iron deficiency anaemia and dysphagia", and then withdraws it as an explanation: "the pathophysiology remains elusive, and the association of iron deficiency is also controversial. Possible mechanisms include iron and nutritional deficiencies, genetic predisposition and autoimmunity."​B&L 66 · p.1147 Iron is still listed first in treatment, so the clinical act is unchanged.
Why this is a real difference and not a quibble
If the iron deficiency causes the web, correcting it should resolve the dysphagia, and no dilatation would be needed. All three books in fact hedge on exactly this point by offering dilatation "if necessary" after iron. So the treatment is the same either way; what differs is what you say when asked why the web forms.
How to answer: describe the syndrome as a triad, which no book disputes, and be careful about causation. "Plummer-Vinson syndrome, or Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome in the UK, is the triad of a postcricoid or cervical oesophageal web, iron deficiency anaemia and dysphagia. It occurs almost exclusively in middle-aged women. It is premalignant, predisposing to postcricoid cervical oesophageal cancer, so oesophagoscopy and biopsy are needed to exclude malignancy. Treatment is iron, diet, and endoscopic dilatation of the web if necessary." Then, if pushed on mechanism: "the association with iron deficiency is in the definition but the pathophysiology is not settled; iron and nutritional deficiency, genetic predisposition and autoimmunity have all been proposed." Giving the triad and then conceding the mechanism is unsettled reads as knowing the literature, not as not knowing the answer.
Carcinoma of the oesophagus: is five-year survival 10%, or 40 to 50%? A live disagreement, and the gap is explained entirely by what is being measured. SRB 19 p.802 gives 10%; B&L 66 p.1146 gives 40 to 50%
SRB
Blunt: "difficult approach, late presentation. Nodal involvement carries bad prognosis. 5-year survival rate is only 10%."​SRB 19 · p.802 Its only mention of multimodality treatment is conditional: "neoadjuvant therapy by chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy prior to surgery may improve the survival."​SRB 19 · p.798
Bailey & Love 28e
Four to five times better, with conditions attached: "results from surgical resection alone have improved. Mortality from surgery is less than 5% in dedicated centres... since the 1990s, multimodality treatment has gained impetus and is now routine for advanced disease. Neoadjuvant therapy is more popular than postoperative therapy... overall, after treatment in a multimodality programme, a 5-year survival rate of 40–50% is expected. The disease stage and the ability to perform an R0 resection are the most powerful predictors of outcome."​B&L 66 · p.1146
They are not contradicting each other
Read B&L's sentence again: the 40 to 50% is for patients who reached a multimodality programme and had an R0 resection in a dedicated centre. That is a selected minority. SRB's 10% is closer to survival across all patients with the diagnosis, most of whom present late with unresectable disease, which both books say is the norm. B&L's own explanation for the poor prognosis is the same as SRB's: "late presentation and early spread are reasons for poor prognosis" and "early diagnosis has the best chance of cure".​B&L 66 · p.1146
How to answer: never give a bare survival figure for this cancer. Give the denominator. "Overall five-year survival is poor, of the order of 10%, because most patients present late with unresectable disease. In the selected group who complete a multimodality programme and achieve an R0 resection in a specialist centre, five-year survival of 40 to 50% is reported, and operative mortality in such centres is under 5%. Stage and the ability to achieve an R0 resection are the strongest predictors." That single answer uses both books, cannot be marked wrong by either, and demonstrates exactly the thing the question is testing: that you know a survival figure is meaningless without knowing who is counted in it.
Dysphagia lusoria: a cause in infancy, or one presenting after 40? And B&L has dropped it Part live disagreement, part edition note. S Das 31 pp.434, 441 lists it among infantile causes; SRB 19 p.779 says it usually presents after 40; the word does not appear in B&L 66 at all
S Das
Puts it in the age list for the newborn: "in infancy the common causes of dysphagia are oesophageal atresia, dysphagia lusoria and congenital cardiospasm."​Das 31 · p.434
SRB
The opposite end of life: "commonly they are asymptomatic. Presentations may be dysphagia, chest pain, stridor, wheeze, recurrent respiratory infection (usually presents after the age of 40)."​SRB 19 · p.779
Bailey & Love 28e
Neither "dysphagia lusoria" nor an aberrant right subclavian artery appears anywhere in chapter 66. Nor does Bayford, whom S Das credits with first recognising it. This is an edition and emphasis note rather than a disagreement: B&L has simply not covered a rare congenital cause in a chapter organised around motility, reflux, Barrett's, cancer and perforation. It is not that B&L denies it exists.
Reconciling the two ages
The anomaly is congenital, so the cause is present from birth and S Das is right to put it on an infant's list. A complete vascular ring can obstruct an infant's trachea and oesophagus. But the common form, an aberrant right subclavian running behind the oesophagus, compresses a compliant tube only gradually, and SRB is right that most such patients are asymptomatic until the vessel stiffens or dilates in middle age. Both statements describe the same anomaly at different severities.
One caution about the date in S Das
S Das writes that dysphagia lusoria "was first recognized by Bayford in 1974".​Das 31 · p.441 Bayford was an eighteenth-century English surgeon and the year is a misprint. Do not write 1974 in an answer, and do not offer a date at all unless asked: none of the three books gives a date you can rely on.
How to answer: name the anomaly, not the age. "Dysphagia lusoria is dysphagia caused by an aberrant right subclavian artery arising from the descending aorta and passing behind the oesophagus, from failure of the proximal rather than the distal part of the right fourth aortic arch to involute. Lusoria means a sport of nature. It is congenital, so it can obstruct in infancy, particularly when there is a complete vascular ring, but most patients are asymptomatic and the common presentation is dysphagia after the age of forty. Barium swallow shows a diagonal impression at the level of T4 and endoscopy shows a pulsating extraluminal compression. Treatment is ligation or reconstruction of the aberrant artery." If you list causes of dysphagia in infancy, include it, because S Das does and that is what an Indian examiner has read. Do not expect to find it in Bailey and Love 28e.

7Rapid-fire viva

Define dysphagia and odynophagia.

Dysphagia is difficulty in swallowing. Odynophagia is painful swallowing.​SRB 19 · p.778

What four questions would you ask first?

Age; duration; solids first or liquids first; and whether it is progressive or intermittent. Those four separate the main causes before any examination. Then regurgitation and its timing, pain, cough in relation to meals, and weight loss.​Das 31 · pp.434, 435

Solids first, then liquids. What does that tell you, and why?

Mechanical obstruction, most often carcinoma of the oesophagus, because a fixed narrowing still lets fluid through but arrests a solid bolus. The reverse pattern, liquids before solids, suggests achalasia, because the weight of a solid bolus helps overcome the unrelaxing sphincter.​Das 31 · p.434 Bailey and Love notes achalasia often causes dysphagia to both, so do not reject it on the pattern.​B&L 66 · p.1121

Does the site where the patient feels food sticking tell you the level?

No. SRB is explicit that the site of the food-getting-stuck feeling is not relevant.​SRB 19 · p.778 What does localise is coughing while swallowing, which points to failure of the pharyngeal phase, where laryngeal closure is part of the same reflex.

Classify the causes of dysphagia.

By site, then by layer. In the mouth: tonsillitis, quinsy, stomatitis, carcinoma of the tongue, soft palate palsy. In the pharynx: in the lumen a foreign body; in the wall pharyngitis, malignancy, hysterical spasm, Paterson-Kelly syndrome; outside the wall a retropharyngeal abscess, nodes or a malignant thyroid. In the oesophagus: in the lumen a foreign body; in the wall atresia, benign stricture, spasm including achalasia and webs, diverticulum, neoplasm, neurological causes and Crohn's; outside the wall a goitre, an aortic aneurysm, a mediastinal mass, dysphagia lusoria and a paraoesophageal hiatus hernia.​Das 31 · p.437 Add SRB's neurological column: bulbar palsy, stroke, motor neuron disease, Parkinson's; and oesophageal candidiasis.​SRB 19 · pp.778, 779

One clinical sign you must not omit in a case of dysphagia.

Palpation of the left supraclavicular fossa. S Das: it may be the only sign in carcinoma of the oesophagus.​Das 31 · p.435 The reason is that the thoracic duct drains into the junction of the left jugular and left subclavian veins, which is why a metastatic node appears there, Virchow's node or Troisier's sign.​B&L 66 · p.1108

Which investigation would you do first, and why?

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, in an adult with progressive dysphagia, because it sees the mucosa and gives a biopsy at the same sitting, and carcinoma is what must be excluded.​B&L 66 · p.1108 A contrast swallow first for a suspected pharyngeal pouch, a suspected high or tight stricture, or a suspected motility disorder.

What would you expect on barium swallow in carcinoma, and how does it differ from a benign stricture?

In carcinoma, an irregular filling defect, little dilatation above, shouldering at the proximal end and a soft tissue shadow. In benign stricture, a long tortuous narrowing with some proximal dilatation and no shouldering. Shouldering is the discriminator.​Das 31 · pp.436, 439

Four radiological signs of achalasia.

A bird's beak or smooth pencil-shaped taper at the oesophagogastric junction; dilatation of the oesophagus above it with retained contents; absence of the fundic gas bubble, because no air passes the sphincter; and in late disease a sigmoid or megaoesophagus.​Das 31 · p.436​SRB 19 · p.789​B&L 66 · p.1121 A lateral chest film may show an air-fluid level in the posterior mediastinum.​Das 31 · p.436

A normal endoscopy in a patient you suspect has achalasia. What now?

It does not exclude it: 30 to 40% of endoscopies are reported normal before achalasia is finally diagnosed.​B&L 66 · p.1122 Proceed to manometry, which is the definitive test. The endoscopy was still necessary, to exclude pseudoachalasia, meaning carcinoma of the gastric cardia mimicking achalasia.​B&L 66 · p.1122

What is the gold standard for diagnosing achalasia?

Manometry. Classically a raised resting lower oesophageal sphincter pressure over 35 mmHg with failure of relaxation and absent peristalsis.​SRB 19 · p.790 Current practice is high-resolution manometry, where an abnormal integrated relaxation pressure defines a disorder of oesophagogastric junction outflow under the Chicago classification, and achalasia is divided into three types.​B&L 66 · pp.1121, 1125

Why does type of achalasia matter?

Because type III has a spastic distal segment that responds less well to pneumatic dilatation and to a standard Heller's myotomy, and is better treated by a long myotomy, which peroral endoscopic myotomy can extend proximally.​B&L 66 · pp.1124, 1125

Treatment options in achalasia.

The goal is palliation of symptoms; nothing reverses the neuronal degeneration.​B&L 66 · p.1122 Drugs, calcium channel blockers and nitrates, with limited efficacy and reserved for poor operative candidates. Botulinum toxin into the sphincter, temporary and restricted to the elderly with comorbidity. Graded pneumatic dilatation with 30 to 40 mm balloons. Laparoscopic modified Heller's cardiomyotomy with a partial fundoplication. POEM. And oesophagectomy for end-stage sigmoid or megaoesophagus.​B&L 66 · pp.1123, 1124​SRB 19 · p.790

Why add a partial and not a total fundoplication to a Heller's myotomy?

Because reflux occurs in up to 40% after myotomy, so an antireflux procedure is needed; but a complete 360 degree Nissen wrap is contraindicated, since the increased outflow resistance against an aperistaltic oesophageal body would cause postoperative dysphagia. A Dor anterior or Toupet posterior partial wrap is used.​B&L 66 · p.1124

What is the commonest complication of POEM?

Reflux. Without an antireflux procedure the incidence of oesophagitis at three months can be as high as 57%, which may mean lifelong acid suppression or a later antireflux operation.​B&L 66 · p.1124

Is achalasia premalignant?

Yes, for squamous cell carcinoma, through stasis and persistent retention oesophagitis. SRB quotes a sevenfold risk and around 8% at fifteen years.​SRB 19 · p.789 Bailey and Love lists achalasia among the aetiological factors for squamous cancer but says only that it may predispose,​B&L 66 · pp.1121, 1136 and recommends no surveillance. Practically, endoscopy and biopsy before treating any achalasia, particularly in an older patient.

What is Plummer-Vinson syndrome, and why does it matter?

The triad of a cervical or postcricoid oesophageal web, iron deficiency anaemia and dysphagia, also called Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome in the UK and sideropenic dysphagia.​B&L 66 · p.1146 Almost exclusively middle-aged women. Glossitis with a smooth pale tongue devoid of papillae, cheilitis and koilonychia.​Das 31 · p.438​SRB 19 · p.791 It matters because it is premalignant, predisposing to postcricoid cervical oesophageal cancer.​B&L 66 · p.1147 Treatment: iron, diet, and endoscopic dilatation of the web if necessary, with biopsy to exclude malignancy.

How do you distinguish an oesophageal web from a Schatzki's ring?

By what lines each surface. In a web both the proximal and distal surfaces are squamous. In a Schatzki's ring the proximal side is squamous and the distal side columnar, because it sits at the squamocolumnar junction.​B&L 66 · p.1147 A web is at the top of the oesophagus, a Schatzki's ring at the bottom, where it is a common cause of food impaction. Dysphagia occurs when the ring is under 13 mm.

Where does a pharyngeal pouch arise, and is it a true diverticulum?

Posteriorly, above the cricopharyngeal sphincter, through the dehiscence of Killian between the oblique thyropharyngeal and transverse cricopharyngeal fibres of the inferior constrictor. It is a false pulsion diverticulum: only mucosa and submucosa herniate, so there is no muscle in its wall.​B&L 66 · p.1126​Das 31 · p.438

How would you treat a pharyngeal pouch, and what step is never omitted?

Diverticulectomy through a left cervical incision, since most point to the left; or diverticular suspension, inverting the pouch upwards, which avoids a suture line and so a leak; or transoral stapled division of the septum between pouch and oesophagus. Cricopharyngeus myotomy is an integral part of all of them,​B&L 66 · p.1127 because the cause is failure of coordinated sphincter opening, and excising the pouch without the myotomy leaves the cause behind.

Which oesophageal diverticulum is a true diverticulum, and why?

The midoesophageal or traction diverticulum, near the tracheal bifurcation. It is pulled outwards by fibrosis or lymphadenopathy, classically tuberculous nodes, so the full thickness of the wall is drawn out. Pulsion diverticula, the pharyngeal pouch and the epiphrenic, are pushed out from within and contain only mucosa and submucosa.​B&L 66 · p.1127​Das 31 · pp.439, 440

An epiphrenic diverticulum. What must you look for before operating?

An underlying motility disorder, because epiphrenic diverticula are pulsion diverticula commonly associated with achalasia or another cause of outflow obstruction. A barium oesophagogram shows the diverticulum and screens for the motility disorder, and large diverticula are excised with a myotomy from the neck of the diverticulum to the cardia to relieve the functional obstruction.​B&L 66 · p.1127

A patient with known oesophageal cancer coughs on drinking water. What has happened?

An oesophago-airway fistula. Bailey and Love: choking and cough on drinking water are typical of fistulation, and associated haemoptysis is common.​B&L 66 · p.1136 It indicates advanced, generally unresectable disease and the aim becomes palliation.

Which cell type of oesophageal cancer is commoner, and where?

Squamous cell carcinoma still predominates in the East and in India; Barrett's adenocarcinoma is commoner in the West, where the incidence of adenocarcinoma overtook squamous cancer after the 1990s with the rise in obesity, reflux and Barrett's.​B&L 66 · pp.1135, 1146 Squamous tends to sit in the middle and upper oesophagus, adenocarcinoma in the lower oesophagus and at the oesophagogastric junction.​B&L 66 · p.1136

Name the risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus.

Smoking and alcohol; hot beverages; N-nitroso-containing foods such as pickled vegetables; betel nut chewing; yerba mate; deficiency of fresh fruit, green vegetables and vitamins; low socioeconomic class; fungal toxins or virus; previous mediastinal radiation; lye corrosive stricture; a previous upper aerodigestive malignancy; Plummer-Vinson syndrome; and achalasia.​B&L 66 · p.1136 Barrett's oesophagus, reflux and obesity are risks for adenocarcinoma, not squamous.

Why does oesophageal cancer have such a poor prognosis?

Late presentation and early spread. Early cancers are asymptomatic; the wall lacks a serosa so there is no barrier to local invasion; and a rich submucosal lymphatic plexus allows longitudinal submucosal spread with unpredictable nodal involvement and skip lesions.​B&L 66 · pp.1107, 1108, 1136 That plexus is also why a longer resection margin reduces local recurrence, and the rationale for three-field lymphadenectomy.

What is the five-year survival?

It depends entirely on who is counted. Overall about 10%, because most patients present late and unresectable.​SRB 19 · p.802 In the selected group completing a multimodality programme with an R0 resection in a dedicated centre, 40 to 50%, with operative mortality under 5%. Stage and the ability to achieve an R0 resection are the strongest predictors.​B&L 66 · p.1146

How much of the lumen must be involved before dysphagia appears?

SRB: two-thirds of the lumen blocked by tumour.​SRB 19 · p.778 S Das puts it in terms of circumference and later in the illness: by the time the patient has difficulty with semisolids, three-quarters of the circumference has been involved.​Das 31 · p.441 Either figure makes the same point, that dysphagia is a late symptom, which is why the prognosis is poor.

How would you palliate dysphagia in an unresectable cancer?

A self-expanding metallic stent, which is simple, effective and gives immediate relief; its risks are migration, tumour ingrowth, airway compression and tracheal erosion if placed in the mid or upper oesophagus. Other options are dilatation, laser, photodynamic therapy, and chemotherapy or radiotherapy to restore patency; radiotherapy is also haemostatic in a bleeding junctional tumour.​B&L 66 · p.1146

A corrosive stricture. Acid or alkali, and why does it matter?

Usually alkali, because squamous mucosa is relatively resistant to acid; alkali causes liquefactive necrosis and deeper injury.​SRB 19 · p.778 It matters twice: it predicts the severity of the stricture, and lye corrosive stricture is a recognised risk factor for later squamous cell carcinoma.​B&L 66 · p.1136

Commonest cause of oesophageal perforation?

Iatrogenic, from endoscopic procedures, particularly dilatation of a stricture or of achalasia.​B&L 66 · p.1127 Spontaneous emetogenic perforation, Boerhaave's syndrome, results from a sudden rise in oesophageal pressure against a closed glottis during vomiting.

Which is the commonest form of oesophageal atresia, and how do you confirm it?

Atresia with a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula, about 90% of cases: the proximal oesophagus ends blind and the distal oesophagus joins the lower trachea. The infant has excess frothy saliva, spits up or vomits on feeding, and may choke or become cyanosed. A nasogastric tube is arrested in the upper mediastinum, and a plain film with the radio-opaque tube in situ confirms it; gas in the intestine confirms the distal fistula.​Das 31 · pp.437, 438

Why does scleroderma affect the lower oesophagus rather than the upper?

Because the upper third of the oesophagus is striated muscle and the lower third smooth muscle, and connective tissue disease affects smooth muscle.​B&L 66 · p.1107 Fibrous replacement of the smooth muscle costs the distal oesophagus its tone and its response to swallowing, so reflux follows.​Das 31 · p.439

Where are the three normal constrictions of the oesophagus, and at what distance from the incisors?

At the cricopharyngeus, the upper oesophageal sphincter, about 15 cm; where the aorta and left main bronchus cross it, about 25 cm; and at the oesophagogastric junction, the lower oesophageal sphincter, about 40 cm.​B&L 66 · p.1107 These are where a foreign body impacts and where a corrosive stricture forms.

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love the oesophagus is chapter 66, pp.1106 to 1147. The history and examination are S Das ch.31, which is the only one of the three written as a bedside method. SRB ch.19 supplies the Indian exam framework, including the causes table and the achalasia and Plummer-Vinson sections. Bailey & Love supplies the mechanism and the current management, and it has moved furthest from the other two: it has replaced conventional manometry with high-resolution manometry and the Chicago classification, mentions "barium swallow" only once in forty-two pages, and states that rigid oesophagoscopy is now used only for retrieving foreign bodies. Seven amber boxes set out where the three books genuinely part company.
